name: Superior vena cava
func: The large vein that returns oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest to the right atrium of the heart. It's the top of the two main veins feeding the heart.

levels.kid:
After blood delivers oxygen to your body, it has to come back to your heart for a refill. The **superior vena cava** is one of the two giant veins that bring it home. "Superior" means "upper," because this one collects blood from the top half of you: your head, your brain, your neck and your arms.

It's a short, fat tube that runs down the right side of your chest and plugs into the top of the heart's upper-right room.

It has no doors inside it, so blood just flows straight down into your heart, helped along by gravity when you're standing up.
levels.hs:
The **superior vena cava (SVC)** is a short, wide vein, about 7 cm long and 2 cm across. It forms behind the **right first costal cartilage**, where the **right and left brachiocephalic veins** join. Each brachiocephalic vein is itself formed by the **internal jugular vein** (from the head and neck) and the **subclavian vein** (from the arm) on that side.

The SVC runs straight down on the **right side** of the upper chest, to the right of the **ascending aorta** and in front of the **right main bronchus**, and enters the top of the **right atrium** at about the level of the third costal cartilage. The lower half of it lies inside the pericardium.

Just before it enters the pericardium, it receives the **azygos vein**, which arches forward over the root of the right lung, bringing blood from the back of the chest wall.

The SVC has **no valves**, so the pressure inside it reflects pressure in the right atrium. Doctors use this when they look at the neck veins.
levels.college:
Relations: the SVC is anterior to the right lung root, lateral to the ascending aorta, and medial to the **right phrenic nerve** and the mediastinal pleura. The **right paratracheal lymph nodes** lie close behind it, an important point because enlarged nodes can compress it.

The **sinoatrial (SA) node**, the heart's natural pacemaker, sits in the wall of the right atrium at the **junction of the SVC and the right atrium**, near the top of a groove called the sulcus terminalis. Surgeons operating at this junction must protect it.

The SVC is the target for **central venous catheters**: lines inserted through the internal jugular or subclavian veins, or **PICC lines** from an arm vein, are positioned so their tip sits in the lower SVC or at the cavoatrial junction, roughly at the level of the **carina** on chest X-ray.

If the SVC is blocked, blood finds detours through **collateral pathways**: mainly the **azygos–hemiazygos system**, the **internal thoracic veins**, the **lateral thoracic** and chest wall veins, and the vertebral venous plexuses. Whether the azygos vein is above or below the blockage matters a lot: an obstruction below the azygos forces blood to travel down to the IVC system to return.
levels.phd:
Embryologically, the SVC develops from the **right common cardinal vein** and the proximal **right anterior cardinal vein**. The left brachiocephalic vein forms from an oblique anastomosis between the two anterior cardinal veins; the left common cardinal vein regresses to become the small **oblique vein of the left atrium** and the **coronary sinus**.

If the left anterior cardinal vein fails to regress, a **persistent left superior vena cava** results, in about 0.3–0.5% of people, and far more often in those with congenital heart disease. It usually drains into a markedly **dilated coronary sinus**. Typically harmless, it matters when cardiologists try to place pacemaker leads from the left arm, or when an unexplained big coronary sinus shows up on echo.

The myocardium of the atria extends as **myocardial sleeves** onto the SVC for a short distance. Like the pulmonary vein sleeves, these sleeves can harbor triggering foci for **atrial fibrillation**, so electrophysiologists sometimes electrically isolate the SVC.

Vein walls have a thin media with fewer smooth muscle cells than arteries; the SVC's thin, compliant wall collapses easily under external pressure. Mechanically, venous return depends on the **pressure gradient from peripheral veins to the right atrium** (Guyton's model): mean systemic filling pressure minus right atrial pressure, divided by venous resistance. Breathing in lowers intrathoracic pressure, increasing flow into the SVC.
levels.expert:
**SVC syndrome** results from obstruction, today most commonly by **malignancy** (lung cancer, especially small-cell, and lymphoma) and increasingly by **thrombosis around catheters or pacemaker leads**. Signs: **swelling of the face, neck and arms**, a dusky or plethoric face, distended neck and chest-wall veins that don't collapse, breathlessness, and headache made worse by bending forward. **Pemberton's sign**: raising both arms above the head worsens facial congestion. Severe cases can cause **cerebral edema** and airway narrowing, true emergencies.

The neurosurgical link: raised SVC pressure is transmitted to the jugular veins and dural venous sinuses, impairing cerebral venous drainage and raising **intracranial pressure**. That's also why patients with raised ICP are nursed head-up with the neck straight and why tight cervical collars or ties around the neck are avoided.

Imaging: contrast-enhanced **CT** shows the cause, level and collaterals; venography guides intervention.

Treatment in general terms: head elevation, treating the underlying tumor (chemotherapy or radiotherapy after obtaining tissue diagnosis), **endovascular stenting** for rapid symptom relief, anticoagulation and catheter removal for thrombosis-related cases. **Central line** placement errors near the SVC, such as perforation or misplaced tips, are a known complication that is checked on chest X-ray after insertion.

keyPoints: Drains head, neck, arms and upper chest into the right atrium
Formed by the two brachiocephalic veins behind the right 1st costal cartilage
Receives the azygos vein; has no valves
SA node lies at the SVC–right atrium junction
Central line tips sit in the lower SVC
SVC syndrome: facial and arm swelling, often from cancer

test.q: The superior vena cava is formed by the union of the:
test.explain: The brachiocephalic veins join behind the right first costal cartilage to form the SVC.

test.q: Which large vein arches over the right lung root to join the back of the SVC?
test.explain: The azygos drains the posterior chest wall and is a key collateral in SVC obstruction.

test.q: The heart's natural pacemaker sits at the junction of the SVC and the:
test.explain: The SA node lies in the right atrial wall at the cavoatrial junction.

test.q: The most common cause of SVC syndrome today is:
choices: Malignancy such as lung cancer or lymphoma
test.explain: Tumors compress or invade the thin-walled SVC; catheter-related thrombosis is the next big cause.

test.q: Raising both arms above the head to worsen facial congestion is ______'s sign.
test.explain: Arm elevation narrows the thoracic inlet, unmasking venous obstruction.
